title: Reading a raw file without changing it

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
A CSV file, short for comma-separated values, is plain text. Nothing in the file says what type each column is.

read_csv(), from the readr package, reads a CSV file. It guesses each column’s type from a sample of its values and prints the guess, the column specification. Values listed in its na argument become NA, R’s code for a missing value; by default the list is the empty string ("", an empty cell) and the text NA. The col_types argument states the types you expect instead of letting readr guess. A value that does not fit its stated type becomes NA, readr warns, and problems() lists each such value with its row and column.

Other formats need other functions. read_excel(), from readxl, reads Excel .xls and .xlsx files, one sheet (one tab of a workbook) at a time, optionally from a stated cell range such as A5:F15. SPSS and SAS are two statistics programs. From haven, read_sav() reads SPSS .sav files and read_xpt() reads SAS transport .xpt files; both keep each column’s label, the description stored with it in the file, as a label attribute (extra information stored with a column).

blocks.label: In plain terms
blocks.html:
A raw file is the data as it first reached you.

The commonest raw file is a CSV. The first line holds the column names. Nothing in it says what type each column is.

So read_csv() has to guess. Then it prints what it decided. Read that report every time. A column you expected to be numbers that comes out as text means some cell in it is not a number.

Two habits keep the guess honest:

  • Name the missing-value codes. If the file uses -99, or “NR”, for “not recorded”, say so in na = c("", "NA", "-99", "NR"). Otherwise -99 is read as a real number.
  • Say what you expect. col_types tells read_csv() which type each column should have.

Reading never changes the file.

blocks.alt: A bar chart with four bars. BMXWT 106, BMXHT 361, BMXBMI 389, BMXWAIST 670 missing values.
blocks.caption: Missing values in four body-measure columns of the NHANES 2021–2023 body measures file, as read_xpt() reads it: weight 106, height 361, BMI 389, waist 670 rows. BMI is missing in exactly the 389 rows that lack a weight or a height. These are counts of rows in the file, not survey estimates.

blocks.alt: A bar chart of three children's heights: S01 at 128, S02 at -99 below the zero line, S03 at 131.
blocks.caption: Heights in the made-up camp file as read_csv() reads them when it is not told the code: child S02’s -99 becomes a height of -99 cm, the bar below zero, and min() returns -99. Declaring na = c(““,”NA”, “-99”) makes it NA, and the shortest measured child is 128 cm.

blocks.label: Illustration 1
blocks.html:
Start with a failure. A school camp team sends you a file. Where a child could not be measured, they typed -99. The values below are made up. Here is the file’s text, held in R as one piece of text that runs over several lines; writeLines() prints it as a file would hold it:

library(readr)
camp_text <- "child_id,height_cm,weight_kg
S01,128,26.0
S02,-99,24.5
S03,131,-99"
writeLines(camp_text)
child_id,height_cm,weight_kg
S01,128,26.0
S02,-99,24.5
S03,131,-99

That is the whole of a CSV file: a header line, then one line per child. Read it with read_csv(). Wrapping the text in I() tells read_csv() that this is the data itself, not the name of a file:

camp <- read_csv(I(camp_text))
camp
Rows: 3 Columns: 3
── Column specification ────────────────────────────────────────────────
Delimiter: ","
chr (1): child_id
dbl (2): height_cm, weight_kg

ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data.
ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message.
# A tibble: 3 × 3
  child_id height_cm weight_kg
  <chr>        <dbl>     <dbl>
1 S01            128      26
2 S02            -99      24.5
3 S03            131     -99

The report says height_cm and weight_kg were read as dbl, numbers. That is true, and it is the trap. -99 is a number, so readr had no reason to object. Ask for the shortest child:

min(camp$height_cm)
[1] -99

A height of -99 cm. Every summary of this column is now wrong, and nothing warned you. Tell read_csv() the code. The vector given to na replaces the default, so keep the empty string and "NA" in it as well:

camp <- read_csv(I(camp_text), na = c("", "NA", "-99"), show_col_types = FALSE)
camp
min(camp$height_cm, na.rm = TRUE)
# A tibble: 3 × 3
  child_id height_cm weight_kg
  <chr>        <dbl>     <dbl>
1 S01            128      26
2 S02             NA      24.5
3 S03            131      NA
[1] 128

The -99s are NA now, and the shortest measured child is 128 cm.

Now a second file from the same camp, where one entry says “not measured” in words:

camp_text_2 <- "child_id,height_cm,weight_kg
S01,128,26.0
S02,not measured,24.5
S03,131,27.5"
camp_2 <- read_csv(I(camp_text_2))
Rows: 3 Columns: 3
── Column specification ────────────────────────────────────────────────
Delimiter: ","
chr (2): child_id, height_cm
dbl (1): weight_kg

ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data.
ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message.

The report says height_cm is chr, text. One word in one cell turned the whole column into text, and mean() of it would fail. Say what you expect instead, with col_types. The function cols() takes one entry per column; col_character() means text and col_double() means numbers. A code such as 0042 read as a number becomes 42, so read codes as text:

camp_2 <- read_csv(
  I(camp_text_2),
  col_types = cols(
    child_id = col_character(),
    height_cm = col_double(),
    weight_kg = col_double()
  )
)
camp_2
Warning message:
One or more parsing issues, call `problems()` on your data frame for
details, e.g.:
  dat <- vroom(...)
  problems(dat)
# A tibble: 3 × 3
  child_id height_cm weight_kg
  <chr>        <dbl>     <dbl>
1 S01            128      26
2 S02             NA      24.5
3 S03            131      27.5

The vroom(...) line is readr’s generic example; read it as your own data frame’s name. Now readr warns, keeps height_cm as numbers, and puts NA where the words were. Ask which values did not fit. The last column of problems() names a temporary file that changes from run to run, so keep the first four, named inside square brackets (<int> marks whole numbers):

problems(camp_2)[c("row", "col", "expected", "actual")]
# A tibble: 1 × 4
    row   col expected actual
  <int> <int> <chr>    <chr>
1     3     2 a double not measured

Row 3 of the file, counting the header line as row 1, column 2: readr expected a number and found “not measured”. You now know the value, and the raw file still says exactly what the camp team typed.

blocks.label: Where this picture breaks
blocks.html:
The camp files are made up and three rows long. In a real file of thousands of rows, a code such as -99 does not stand out by eye, which is the reason to declare it when you read.

Declaring na works only for codes you know about. A file may use 999 for one column and 0 for another, and 0 can be a real value. The codes come from the file’s own documentation, not from guessing; where there is none, ask the person who made the file.

blocks.label: Illustration 2
blocks.html:
Now the real file. Read the penguin data and let read_csv() print its report:

library(readr)
library(here)
penguins_raw <- read_csv(here("data-raw", "penguins_raw.csv"))
here() starts at ~/project
Rows: 344 Columns: 17
── Column specification ────────────────────────────────────────────────
Delimiter: ","
chr  (9): studyName, Species, Region, Island, Stage, Individual ID, ...
dbl  (7): Sample Number, Culmen Length (mm), Culmen Depth (mm), Flip...
date (1): Date Egg

ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data.
ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message.

Read the report line by line. Rows: 344 Columns: 17 gives the size. Delimiter: "," says the values were separated by commas. Then the guesses: nine columns as chr, text; seven as dbl, numbers; one as date. The list after each type is cut short to fit the line. Date Egg became a date because its values are written year-month-day, such as 2007-11-11, which readr recognises.

Check each guess against what you know. Body mass should be a number, and it is in the dbl line. To make that expectation part of the script, name the column in col_types. Columns you do not name are still guessed, unless .default = inside cols() sets the type of every column you do not name:

penguins_raw <- read_csv(
  here("data-raw", "penguins_raw.csv"),
  col_types = cols(`Body Mass (g)` = col_double())
)

It reads quietly. When col_types is given, readr stops printing the report. If a later copy of this file ever arrives with “3750 g” typed in that column, this line warns, and the problems() list names the row.

Last, prove that reading did not touch the file. tools::md5sum() computes an MD5 checksum, a 32-character code calculated from every byte (the units a file is stored in) of a file. Change one character in the file and the code changes. Take it, read the file again, and take it again (unname() drops the file name that md5sum() attaches):

before <- tools::md5sum(here("data-raw", "penguins_raw.csv"))
penguins_raw <- read_csv(here("data-raw", "penguins_raw.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
after <- tools::md5sum(here("data-raw", "penguins_raw.csv"))
unname(before)
unname(before == after)
[1] "049da101568e078f9845c8b366481810"
[1] TRUE

Same code before and after. Write the checksum into the project’s README the day a raw file arrives. Then anyone can check, later, that the file the analysis reads is the file that arrived.

blocks.label: Where this picture breaks
blocks.html:
The checksum shows that the bytes of the file are unchanged since you computed it. It says nothing about whether the data were right when they arrived.

The type report comes from a sample of rows. In a large file, a stray word far down a column may be missed by the guess. Stating col_types for the columns that matter closes that gap.

blocks.label: Illustration 3
blocks.html:
Not every raw file is a CSV. Here are the three other kinds this book’s reader meets most.

Excel. The readxl package comes with a small example workbook that is laid out the way people lay out sheets for printing, with notes above and below the table. readxl_example() gives the address of that file. Read it without instructions and count the rows:

library(readxl)
nrow(read_excel(readxl_example("deaths.xlsx")))
New names:
• `` -> `...2`
• `` -> `...3`
• `` -> `...4`
• `` -> `...5`
• `` -> `...6`
[1] 18

readxl gave the blank headers made-up names such as ...2. The notes became rows: 18 rows, the real header row among them, and every column text. Give the sheet and the cells that hold the table:

read_excel(readxl_example("deaths.xlsx"), sheet = "other", range = "A5:F15")
# A tibble: 10 × 6
   Name           Profession   Age `Has kids` `Date of birth`
   <chr>          <chr>      <dbl> <lgl>      <dttm>
 1 Vera Rubin     scientist     88 TRUE       1928-07-23 00:00:00
 2 Mohamed Ali    athlete       74 TRUE       1942-01-17 00:00:00
 3 Morley Safer   journalist    84 TRUE       1931-11-08 00:00:00
 4 Fidel Castro   politician    90 TRUE       1926-08-13 00:00:00
 5 Antonin Scalia lawyer        79 TRUE       1936-03-11 00:00:00
 6 Jo Cox         politician    41 TRUE       1974-06-22 00:00:00
 7 Janet Reno     lawyer        78 FALSE      1938-07-21 00:00:00
 8 Gwen Ifill     journalist    61 FALSE      1955-09-29 00:00:00
 9 John Glenn     astronaut     95 TRUE       1921-07-28 00:00:00
10 Pat Summit     coach         64 TRUE       1952-06-14 00:00:00
# ℹ 1 more variable: `Date of death` <dttm>

Now there is one header row and ten rows of data. Ages are numbers, <lgl> marks TRUE or FALSE, and the two date columns are <dttm>, date-times, printed with a time of midnight that readxl attaches. If you want to look at an Excel file before reading it, open a copy and leave the original alone.

SPSS. The haven package comes with an SPSS copy of a classic dataset of iris flowers. system.file() finds a file installed with a package:

library(haven)
iris_spss <- read_sav(system.file("examples", "iris.sav", package = "haven"))
head(iris_spss, 3)
# A tibble: 3 × 5
  Sepal.Length Sepal.Width Petal.Length Petal.Width Species
         <dbl>       <dbl>        <dbl>       <dbl> <dbl+lbl>
1          5.1         3.5          1.4         0.2 1 [setosa]
2          4.9         3            1.4         0.2 1 [setosa]
3          4.7         3.2          1.3         0.2 1 [setosa]

Look at Species. Its type is dbl+lbl, a number with a label: SPSS stored the number 1 and the label setosa, and haven keeps both. Missing-value codes declared inside an SPSS file become NA when it is read, unless you ask otherwise.

SAS transport. NHANES, the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey of the United States, publishes its files as .xpt. This book’s project holds the body measures file of the 2021–2023 cycle. Both files are on the NHANES data pages of the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention; download BMX_L.xpt and DEMO_L.xpt into data-raw/. Read the body measures file with read_xpt(), and its weight column’s label with attr(), which reads an attribute:

bmx <- read_xpt(here("data-raw", "BMX_L.xpt"))
dim(bmx)
attr(bmx$BMXWT, "label")
[1] 8860   22
[1] "Weight (kg)"

The file has 8860 rows, one per person examined, and 22 columns. The column names are codes, and the label carries their meaning: BMXWT is weight in kg. The label came with the file; nobody typed it. Look at the labels of four columns, and count the missing values in each. bmx[c(...)] keeps the named columns. sapply() asks each column in turn for its label, and colSums() adds up the missing values column by column:

body <- bmx[c("BMXWT", "BMXHT", "BMXBMI", "BMXWAIST")]
sapply(body, attr, "label")
colSums(is.na(body))
                      BMXWT                       BMXHT
              "Weight (kg)"      "Standing Height (cm)"
                     BMXBMI                    BMXWAIST
"Body Mass Index (kg/m**2)"  "Waist Circumference (cm)"
   BMXWT    BMXHT   BMXBMI BMXWAIST
     106      361      389      670

BMI is missing more often than weight or height. The documentation says BMI was calculated from weight and height, so it is missing whenever either one is. Check that, with | meaning “or”:

sum(is.na(bmx$BMXWT) | is.na(bmx$BMXHT))
[1] 389

Exactly 389 rows lack a weight or a height, the same as the rows that lack a BMI. The four counts also match the code tables printed in the survey’s own codebook (its published description of every column, with a count for each value). These are counts of rows in the file, unweighted. They are not survey estimates (figures for the whole US population): the survey’s documentation says its sample weights should be used to analyse these data, and no count or average in this book uses them. Sample weights are columns of the demographics file, nothing to do with body weight; another book of this series teaches them.

blocks.label: Where this picture breaks
blocks.html:
The Excel and SPSS files are examples that come inside the readxl and haven packages. Their contents are not health data; they are there to show the reading.

The NHANES counts describe the people examined in one American survey cycle, at all ages, infants included. They say nothing about how many people in India, or in the United States, lack a measurement.

points.html: The error is to think that a file which reads without an error has been read correctly. -99 read as a height raises no warning. Read the column report, and declare every missing-value code from the file’s documentation in na before you compute anything.
Giving na replaces the default list. Write na = c("", "NA", "-99"), not na = "-99"; the second form stops reading empty cells and the text “NA” as missing.
A number column that the report calls chr holds at least one value that is not a number. Never open the raw file and retype the cell.
Record the MD5 checksum of every raw file in the README on the day it arrives.
Open an Excel file you were sent only as a copy. Read the original into R with read_excel(), giving the sheet and range.
When a department hands over an SPSS file, read it with read_sav() rather than asking for an Excel export.
Any average you compute from an NHANES file without its sample weights (columns of the demographics file, nothing to do with body weight) describes the people in the file only.
Reading carefully catches codes and types. It cannot catch a wrong value that is a valid number: a height of 182 cm typed for 128 cm reads perfectly.

blocks.prompt: Without looking back, write the argument that makes read_csv() treat -99 as missing without losing its default missing values. Then name the function that lists the values that did not fit the types given in col_types.
blocks.answer:
na = c("", "NA", "-99"). Giving na replaces the default list, which is the empty string and the text “NA”, so both go back in beside -99.

problems(), called on the data frame that read_csv() returned. It gives the row, the column, the type expected and the value found.

blocks.prompt:
A district team sends you screening_2026.csv, exported from their form. Its documentation says four things:

  • height and weight are in cm and kg;
  • 999 means “not measured”;
  • “NR” means “not recorded”;
  • village_code is a code with leading zeros, such as 0042.

Write the reading line, with every argument you need, and say what each argument protects you from.
blocks.answer:
library(readr)
library(here)
screening <- read_csv(
  here("data-raw", "screening_2026.csv"),
  na = c("", "NA", "999", "NR"),
  col_types = cols(
    village_code = col_character(),
    height_cm = col_double(),
    weight_kg = col_double()
  )
)
problems(screening)
  • here("data-raw", ...): the address works on any computer that has the project.
  • na: 999 and “NR” become NA, so 999 cm never enters a summary. The empty string and “NA” stay in the list, because giving na replaces the default.
  • village_code = col_character(): read as a number, 0042 would become 42. Read as text, it stays 0042, as the documentation writes it.
  • height_cm and weight_kg as col_double(): any word typed in those columns is reported by problems() instead of turning the column into text.

Columns not named in cols() are still guessed. The block is shown, not run, because the file is made up.

blocks.prompt:
You read a made-up clinic file and read_csv() prints this report:

Rows: 1250 Columns: 6, then chr (3): patient_id, sex, weight_kg and dbl (3): age_years, height_cm, visit_no.

What does the report tell you, what does it not tell you, and what do you do next?
blocks.answer:
It tells you the file has 1250 rows and 6 columns, and that weight_kg was read as text. Weight should be a number. So at least one cell in that column is not a number. It may hold a unit (“62 kg”), a word (“absent”), or a comma used as a decimal mark.

It does not tell you which cells, how many, or whether the other numbers are right. It does not tell you whether 1250 rows means 1250 patients.

Next, read again with col_types = cols(weight_kg = col_double()). Run problems() to list the cells that are not numbers, and decide in code what each means. If they are a missing-value code, add it to na.

blocks.prompt:
Read this made-up CSV text with read_csv() and print the result. Wrap the text in I().

"district,children,with_obesity
Raipur,410,23
Durg,385,19"
blocks.answer:
library(readr)
read_csv(I("district,children,with_obesity
Raipur,410,23
Durg,385,19"))
Rows: 2 Columns: 3
── Column specification ────────────────────────────────────────────────
Delimiter: ","
chr (1): district
dbl (2): children, with_obesity

ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data.
ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message.
# A tibble: 2 × 3
  district children with_obesity
  <chr>       <dbl>        <dbl>
1 Raipur        410           23
2 Durg          385           19

Two rows and three columns. district is text; the two counts are numbers.

blocks.prompt:
Read this made-up text with col_types given as a short string, one letter per column: c for text and d for numbers. Print the result.

"ward,beds,occupied
A,30,27
B,24,24"
blocks.answer:
library(readr)
read_csv(I("ward,beds,occupied
A,30,27
B,24,24"), col_types = "cdd")
# A tibble: 2 × 3
  ward   beds occupied
  <chr> <dbl>    <dbl>
1 A        30       27
2 B        24       24

The string "cdd" says: first column text, second and third numbers. No report is printed, because the types were given.

blocks.prompt: Read the Excel example workbook that comes with readxl, readxl_example("deaths.xlsx"), taking only the cells A5:C8 of the sheet called arts. How many rows and columns do you get?
blocks.answer:
library(readxl)
read_excel(readxl_example("deaths.xlsx"), range = "arts!A5:C8")
# A tibble: 3 × 3
  Name          Profession   Age
  <chr>         <chr>      <dbl>
1 David Bowie   musician      69
2 Carrie Fisher actor         60
3 Chuck Berry   musician      90

Three rows and three columns. Row 5 of the sheet became the header, and rows 6 to 8 are data. The sheet can be named inside the range, as arts!, instead of in sheet.

blocks.prompt: Read the penguin file with its column report showing. How many columns were read as text, as numbers and as dates? Which numeric columns would you expect, from their names?
blocks.answer:
library(readr)
library(here)
penguins_raw <- read_csv(here("data-raw", "penguins_raw.csv"))
here() starts at ~/project
Rows: 344 Columns: 17
── Column specification ────────────────────────────────────────────────
Delimiter: ","
chr  (9): studyName, Species, Region, Island, Stage, Individual ID, ...
dbl  (7): Sample Number, Culmen Length (mm), Culmen Depth (mm), Flip...
date (1): Date Egg

ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data.
ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message.

Nine as text (chr), seven as numbers (dbl), one as a date. The seven numeric columns include the four measurements whose names carry a unit, (mm) or (g), and the two isotope ratios. The seventh is Sample Number, a running number, which is stored as a number but is not a measurement.

blocks.prompt: Read the NHANES demographics file, DEMO_L.xpt, from the project’s data-raw folder. Give its number of rows and columns, and the label of the column RIDAGEYR.
blocks.answer:
library(haven)
library(here)
demo <- read_xpt(here("data-raw", "DEMO_L.xpt"))
dim(demo)
attr(demo$RIDAGEYR, "label")
here() starts at ~/project
[1] 11933    27
[1] "Age in years at screening"

11933 rows and 27 columns. RIDAGEYR is age in years at screening. The demographics file has more rows than the body measures file, because not everyone screened was examined.

blocks.prompt:
A resident wants all the measurements read as numbers. She writes this, gets a warning, and notes “child IDs missing in the file”. Run it. Find what broke and why her note looks reasonable. The data are made up.

library(readr)
camp <- read_csv(I("child_id,height_cm,weight_kg
S01,128,26.0
S02,133,24.5
S03,131,27.5"), col_types = cols(.default = col_double()))
camp
Warning message:
One or more parsing issues, call `problems()` on your data frame for
details, e.g.:
  dat <- vroom(...)
  problems(dat)
# A tibble: 3 × 3
  child_id height_cm weight_kg
     <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>
1       NA       128      26
2       NA       133      24.5
3       NA       131      27.5
blocks.answer:
The col_types line broke. .default = col_double() says every column is numbers, including child_id. “S01” is not a number, so every ID became NA. The IDs are in the file. The code threw them away.

Her note looks reasonable because the result shows NA in the ID column, and NA reads as “missing”. The warning said what happened: values did not fit the type she asked for.

Name the ID column as text and let the rest default to numbers:

camp <- read_csv(I("child_id,height_cm,weight_kg
S01,128,26.0
S02,133,24.5
S03,131,27.5"), col_types = cols(child_id = col_character(), .default = col_double()))
camp
# A tibble: 3 × 3
  child_id height_cm weight_kg
  <chr>        <dbl>     <dbl>
1 S01            128      26
2 S02            133      24.5
3 S03            131      27.5

blocks.prompt:
The penguin file has no -99 codes, but a resident adds na = "-99" to be safe. Then she counts the rows with no sex recorded and finds none. Run her code. Find what broke, and why the answer looked believable.

library(readr)
library(here)
penguins_raw <- read_csv(here("data-raw", "penguins_raw.csv"), na = "-99")
sum(is.na(penguins_raw$Sex))
here() starts at ~/project
Rows: 344 Columns: 17
── Column specification ────────────────────────────────────────────────
Delimiter: ","
chr  (15): studyName, Species, Region, Island, Stage, Individual ID,...
dbl   (1): Sample Number
date  (1): Date Egg

ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data.
ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message.
[1] 0
blocks.answer:
The na = "-99" argument broke it. It replaced the default list, so the text “NA” in the file is no longer read as missing. The 11 rows with no sex recorded now have the text “NA” as their sex, which is not NA, so the count is 0. The report gives it away: 15 columns are now chr, because “NA” in a number column is a word, not a number.

The answer looked believable because 0 is a possible count, and nothing stopped. Keep the defaults in the list:

penguins_raw <- read_csv(here("data-raw", "penguins_raw.csv"), na = c("", "NA", "-99"),
                         show_col_types = FALSE)
sum(is.na(penguins_raw$Sex))
[1] 11

Eleven rows have no sex recorded.

blocks.prompt: A slide at a journal club says: “NHANES 2021–2023 measured 8860 people; their mean weight was 70.5 kg.” Check the two numbers against the body measures file, and say what the slide’s sentence does not establish.
blocks.answer:
library(haven)
library(here)
bmx <- read_xpt(here("data-raw", "BMX_L.xpt"))
nrow(bmx)
sum(!is.na(bmx$BMXWT))
mean(bmx$BMXWT, na.rm = TRUE)
min(bmx$BMXWT, na.rm = TRUE)
here() starts at ~/project
[1] 8860
[1] 8754
[1] 70.54904
[1] 2.7

The file has 8860 rows. Only 8754 of them have a weight, so the mean is over 8754 people, not 8860:

8860 − 106 = 8754

The mean of those weights is 70.54904 kg, which rounds to 70.5 kg. So both numbers can be reproduced from the file. The smallest weight is 2.7 kg, an infant: the file covers all ages.

What the sentence does not establish:

  • The average weight of Americans. This mean is unweighted. The survey’s documentation says its sample weights should be used, and they were not.
  • The average weight of adults. Children and infants are in the 8754.
  • Anything about India. It is one survey of the United States.

blocks.prompt: A colleague says: “I only opened the CSV in Excel to look at it and saved it. Nothing changed; it is still the original.” The project’s README recorded the file’s MD5 checksum on the day it arrived: 049da101568e078f9845c8b366481810. Decide what to compute, and compute it for the project’s copy. Then show what a single hand edit does to the checksum, using a copy in output/. Say what the check does not establish.
blocks.answer:
Compute the checksum of the file the analysis reads, and compare it with the one in the README:

library(readr)
library(here)
raw_path <- here("data-raw", "penguins_raw.csv")
unname(tools::md5sum(raw_path)) == "049da101568e078f9845c8b366481810"
here() starts at ~/project
[1] TRUE

TRUE: this copy is byte for byte the file that arrived. Now see what a single change does. Make a copy in output/ and change one character on one line, the way a hand edit would. readLines() reads a file’s lines into a vector, sub() replaces the first match in a piece of text, and writeLines() writes lines to a file:

lines <- readLines(raw_path)
lines[2] <- sub("3750", "3760", lines[2])
dir.create(here("output"), showWarnings = FALSE)
writeLines(lines, here("output", "penguins_edited.csv"))
unname(tools::md5sum(here("output", "penguins_edited.csv")))
[1] "ca70412ca7d8c1908ef8530279c1111f"

One digit changed, and the checksum is completely different. If your colleague’s saved file gives the README’s checksum, nothing changed. If it gives anything else, something did, even if the cells look the same on screen.

What the check does not establish:

  • What changed, or whether it matters. A different checksum says the bytes differ. It does not say which value, or whether a spreadsheet only changed how a date was written.
  • That the original was correct. The checksum only ties today’s file to the day it arrived.
  • Which file the analysis used, if the script reads some other copy. Check the path in the script as well.
